title: The Alphabet V: t ṯ d ḏ
short: The bread loaf t, the tethering rope ṯ, the hand d and the cobra ḏ.
trouble: Students drop the line under ṯ and ḏ. Without it, nṯr "god" becomes a different word.

blocks.html: The last group of one-consonant signs: two t sounds and two d sounds. After this you know the whole alphabet (The Alphabet I: ꜣ j y ꜥ w to here).
The bread loaf 𓏏 t, the tethering rope 𓍿 ṯ, the hand 𓂧 d and the cobra 𓆓 ḏ. The line under ṯ and ḏ makes them different letters.

The bread loaf is one of the most frequent signs of all, because it writes the feminine ending: zꜣ “son”, zꜣt “daughter”. The rope and the cobra write the sounds Egyptologists say “tj” and “dj”. nṯr “god” is said “netjer”; ḏd “say” is said “djed”.

blocks.html: Here are all the one-consonant signs, in dictionary order: 𓄿𓇋𓇌𓂝𓅱𓃀𓊪𓆑𓅓𓈖𓂋𓉔𓎛𓐍𓄡𓊃𓋴𓈙𓈎𓎡𓎼𓏏𓍿𓂧𓆓 = ꜣ j y ꜥ w b p f m n r h ḥ ḫ ẖ z s š q k g t ṯ d ḏ. That is the order of every Egyptian dictionary, as the next lesson shows.

Why does the line matter so much? Because Egyptian has words that differ only by it. Dropping the line turns one consonant into another, just as changing “t” to “d” turns “ten” into “den”. A transliteration without the marks is a different (often meaningless) string.

Dropping the line under ṯ and ḏ. Without it, nṯr “god” would be read with a plain t, which is not the word. When you type, use T for ṯ and D for ḏ. Check the sign: the rope 𓍿 and the cobra 𓆓 always have the line; the loaf and the hand never do.

blocks.html: With all five groups learned, you can already read every word spelled only with one-consonant signs. Most words also use two- and three-consonant signs, which come in the next unit.
